For \(S_n=\left(\frac{n(n+1)}2\right)^2\), let \(T_n=\frac{n(n+1)}2\). Then
\[
d(S_n)=d(T_n^2).
\]
If \(T_n=\prod p_i^{e_i}\), then
\[
d(T_n^2)=\prod (2e_i+1),
\]
so \(m\) must be odd.

For prime \(m>1\), we would need \(T_n=p^{(m-1)/2}\). But \(T_n=\frac{n(n+1)}2\) is a prime power only for \(T_1=1\) and \(T_2=3\). Thus the only prime \(m\) attainable is \(m=3\).

So we only need check odd composite \(m\le 25\): \(9,15,21,25\).

Explicit examples:
\[
\begin{aligned}
T_1&=1 &&\Rightarrow d=1,\\
T_2&=3 &&\Rightarrow d=3,\\
T_3&=6=2\cdot 3 &&\Rightarrow d=3\cdot 3=9,\\
T_7&=28=2^2\cdot 7 &&\Rightarrow d=5\cdot 3=15,\\
T_{16}&=136=2^3\cdot 17 &&\Rightarrow d=7\cdot 3=21,\\
T_8&=36=2^2\cdot 3^2 &&\Rightarrow d=5\cdot 5=25.
\end{aligned}
\]
All other odd \(m\le 25\) are primes \(\ge 5\), which are impossible, and even \(m\) are impossible since \(d(S_n)\) is odd.

Thus the attainable \(m\) are
\[
1,3,9,15,21,25,
\]
so there are \(\boxed{6}\) such positive integers.
